792.title: Satta and Balvand
792.hook: two minstrels who, tradition says, quarreled with Guru Arjan and were forgiven; their Var is in the Granth (Ramkali, ang 966–968)
792.howItsDone: The Var of Satta and Balvand in Raag Ramkali is sung in kirtan like other Gurbani, and Sikhs tell their story as one of pride, return and forgiveness.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Bhatts, who praised the Gurus as one light. Your line was poets of praise. Did you tell someone the goodness you'd seen in them? Day seven hundred ninety-two.

Two musicians, a rebab and a voice, singing kirtan in the Guru's court. Satta and Balvand. Then, tradition says, something goes wrong. A request for money, a quarrel, wounded pride. They stop singing. They say hard things about the house they served. And they walk out. A falling-out could end right there. This one ends with their song inside the Guru Granth Sahib, in Raag Ramkali, Ang 966, kept and sung beside the Gurus' own words.
screen: `TWO MUSICIANS IN THE GURU'S COURT.` → `A QUARREL, AND A WALKOUT.` → `THEIR SONG IN THE GRANTH.`

segments.voice: First the story, as tradition tells it. Satta and Balvand ask Guru Arjan for help, and when it isn't what they hoped, pride takes over. They refuse to play, and they boast that the Gurus' fame rests on their music. Without the court, though, their fortunes sink. In the end they come back, humbled, asking forgiveness, and tradition says a devoted Sikh pleaded for them. The Guru forgives them. They pick up the rebab again. That's the tradition. Now the text, which is what the Granth actually keeps: their Var, a ballad, in Raag Ramkali. And what does it sing about? Not themselves. It sings about Guru Nanak setting up Lehna as the next Guru, Guru Angad, and the line passing on. In paraphrase, one of its lines: the light is the same, the way is the same; the master has only changed the body. It's the claim the Bhatts made yesterday, but listen to who is making it now. Two men who once claimed the Gurus needed them end up singing that the Guru is one light, needing nothing from anyone, passing from body to body. The quarrel was about who mattered. The song answers it: the light matters, and everyone else is a singer. And notice what the Guru did. He didn't just let them back in the door. Their words went into the scripture, to be sung in gurdwaras alongside his own. Forgiveness here isn't a grudging truce. It's a microphone handed back.
screen: `A REQUEST, A QUARREL, A WALKOUT.` · `HUMBLED, THEY COME BACK; THE GURU FORGIVES.` · `THE SAME LIGHT, ONLY THE BODY CHANGED.` · `A MICROPHONE HANDED BACK.` · then, large: `FORGIVEN, AND SUNG.`

segments.voice: The practice: forgive a quarrel. In the sit, choose a small one. Not the deepest wound of your life; something sized for two minutes. A sharp exchange, a slight, a door that closed. Let the other person's face come to mind. You don't have to call them, and you don't have to pretend it didn't happen. Just loosen your grip on it, one breath at a time. If something in you is ready, imagine handing them their voice back. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Satta and Balvand. Two minstrels who, tradition says, quarreled with Guru Arjan and were forgiven. Their Var in Raag Ramkali sings of one light passed from Guru to Guru.
Your line: forgiven, and sung. Today, once, let someone who stepped on your toes back into the conversation, and let them speak. Day seven hundred ninety-two.

793.title: The saloks to Mardana
793.hook: a few saloks are headed with Mardana's name, generally read as Nanak's words to him (Bihagra ki Var, ang 553)
793.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Bhai Mardana as Guru Nanak's companion and rebab player, and the saloks headed with his name in Bihagra ki Var are read and sung as part of that Var.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Satta and Balvand: a quarrel, a return, and a song kept in the Granth. Your line was forgiven, and sung. Did you let someone back into the conversation? Day seven hundred ninety-three.

Mardana. In the Sikh stories he is close by: Guru Nanak's companion on the road, a Muslim musician with a rebab, playing while Nanak sang. Yesterday's minstrels came later. Now open the Guru Granth Sahib to Bihagra ki Var, Ang 553. Among the saloks there, a few carry Mardana's name in the heading. They are generally read as Nanak's words to him, friend to friend. And they are not gentle words.
screen: `MARDANA AND HIS REBAB.` → `HIS NAME IN THE HEADING.` → `NANAK'S WORDS TO A FRIEND.`

segments.voice: The saloks begin with a picture a friend might use to tease you awake. In paraphrase: this dark age is the wine jar, desire is the wine, and the mind is the one drinking it. Anger is the cup, filled with attachment, and ego is the one pouring. Drink in that company, and you're ruined. Strong words. But look where they go next, because Nanak doesn't just take the cup away. He offers a different brew. In paraphrase again: make good deeds the vat, truth the sweetener, and truth itself the finest wine. Make goodness the bread and good conduct the butter. That's the drink, he says, that wipes away wrongdoing. So the saloks don't scold the thirst. They redirect it. Whatever pulls at you, desire, the need to be filled, take that same longing and point it at truth. Now the heading. Readers differ on what the name Mardana is doing there: whether the words are spoken to him, or carry his name for another reason. The tradition generally hears them as words to a friend. And that changes how they sound. These aren't lines shouted at a crowd. They're the kind of thing you say to someone you've walked with for years, who can take hard words because they know you love them. Friends do that. They name the cup in your hand. Then they hand you a better one.
screen: `THE AGE IS THE JAR, DESIRE THE WINE.` · `A DIFFERENT BREW: DEEDS, TRUTH, GOODNESS.` · `NOT SCOLDING THE THIRST: REDIRECTING IT.` · `HARD WORDS, BETWEEN FRIENDS.` · then, large: `WORDS TO A FRIEND.`

segments.voice: For the practice, talk kindly with a friend. In the sit, bring to mind a friend who has walked with you a long way. Think of a moment they told you something true that you didn't want to hear, or a moment you wish you had. Notice how kindness and honesty can sit in the same sentence. Then think of one kind thing you could say to that friend today, true and warm. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
The saloks to Mardana. Saloks in Bihagra ki Var headed with Mardana's name, generally read as Guru Nanak's words to his companion: trade the old cup for the wine of truth.
Your line: words to a friend. Today, send one friend a message that is both kind and true. Day seven hundred ninety-three.

794.title: Sundar's call
794.hook: Sundar records Guru Amar Das's last wishes: sing the Lord's praise, don't weep for me (Ramkali, Sadd, ang 923)
794.howItsDone: At Sikh funerals kirtan and the reading of Gurbani are central, and the Sadd is sometimes sung; Sikh teaching speaks of death as the soul answering God's call home.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the saloks to Mardana: name the cup, then offer a better one. Your line was words to a friend. Did you send one message both kind and true? Day seven hundred ninety-four.

Some families keep a letter in a drawer, written to be opened after a parent dies. Sometimes it holds money matters. Sometimes it says: don't make a fuss, play my favorite song, eat well. In Raag Ramkali, on Ang 923, the Guru Granth Sahib keeps something like that letter. A poet named Sundar records what Guru Amar Das asked of his family as his life came to its end. It's called the Sadd, the call.
screen: `A LETTER IN A DRAWER.` → `PLAY MY SONG, DON'T FUSS.` → `THE SADD, ANG 923.`

segments.voice: In the hymn, the call is the one that comes from God at the end of a life, the summons home. Sundar, whom tradition counts in Guru Amar Das's own family, tells it as an eyewitness would. The Guru gathers his family and speaks plainly. In paraphrase: let no one weep for me after I'm gone; the one who weeps does not please me. Then what he wants instead. In paraphrase again: after me, sing pure kirtan. Send for the Lord's learned ones, and let them read the Lord's story. Let the Lord's Name be heard. And then the line passes on. The Sadd tells how Guru Amar Das names Ram Das as the Guru after him, and the family bows before him. So in one short hymn you get three things side by side: a death, a song, and the light passing on. Look closely at what the Guru asks. He isn't saying grief is wrong for everyone, always. He's saying what he wants for his own going. He sees his death as being called home, so the fitting answer is praise, not wailing. A death, reframed as a summons. And it's recorded by someone close to him, who could have written only his own sorrow, and instead wrote down the instructions. Tradition carries this into Sikh funerals, where kirtan and the reading of Gurbani are given the center, and the evening prayer, Kirtan Sohila, is recited. Grief comes. The Sadd gives it a song to walk alongside.
screen: `SADD: THE CALL HOME.` · `LET NO ONE WEEP FOR ME.` · `KIRTAN, THE LORD'S STORY, THE NAME.` · `A DEATH, A SONG, THE LIGHT PASSED ON.` · then, large: `SING, DON'T WEEP.`

segments.voice: Today's practice: sing instead of mourning, once. Go gently. In the sit, bring to mind someone you've lost, or something that has ended. If tears come, let them; the bell isn't in a hurry. Then find one thing about them that makes you glad. A laugh, a phrase, a song they loved. Let that come forward and fill the breath. If you'd like, hum a line of something you love, even silently. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Sadd. A call, the summons home. Sundar's hymn in Raag Ramkali records Guru Amar Das's wish: when I'm gone, sing the Lord's praise, don't weep for me.
Your line: sing, don't weep. Today, when something sad crosses your mind, let one glad memory sit beside it, and give it a song. Day seven hundred ninety-four.

795.title: Nothing edited out
795.hook: the Gurus kept these voices and sometimes answered them in hymns of their own
795.howItsDone: In the Guru Granth Sahib the Bhagats' compositions appear under their own names, and Sikh teachers point out the places where a Guru's salok stands beside a Bhagat's and takes up its theme.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sundar's call, the Sadd: Guru Amar Das asked his family not to weep, but to sing. Your line was sing, don't weep. Did a glad memory get to sit beside a sad one? Day seven hundred ninety-five.

A shared document, the kind a team writes together. One person types a paragraph. Someone else disagrees. They could delete it and write their own. Or they could leave a comment in the margin: here's how I'd put it. The paragraph stays. The comment sits beside it. Anyone who opens the file later sees both. The Guru Granth Sahib does something like that with the Bhagats, and it keeps both names on the page.
screen: `A SHARED DOCUMENT.` → `DELETE IT, OR COMMENT BESIDE IT?` → `BOTH STAY ON THE PAGE.`

segments.voice: For weeks now we've walked through the Bhagats: Kabir, Namdev, Ravidas, Farid, Ramanand, Jaidev and more. Their words sit in the Granth under their own names. And sometimes, right beside a Bhagat's verse, there's a verse marked with a Guru's name. It happens among Kabir's saloks, and among Farid's. Readers hear some of these as replies. Take one pair, on Ang 1380. Farid says, in paraphrase: cut open my body and not a drop of blood comes out; those steeped in the Lord have no blood left. Right after it, a verse marked with Guru Amar Das's number answers: this body is all blood, and without blood there is no body; what drains from one steeped in the Lord is the blood of greed. Same image, carried a step further. Consider what the compilers could have done instead. If a Bhagat's line said something a Guru would put differently, the easy move was to cut it, or smooth it into the Gurus' own voice. The Granth doesn't. The Bhagat's words keep the Bhagat's name and the Bhagat's way of saying it. The Guru's verse comes in beside it, with the Guru's name. Two voices, both visible. A reader gets the conversation, not just the conclusion. That says something about the Granth itself. It isn't the record of one voice talking to itself. It's a house with many speakers, where the Gurus' voice leads and others are honored at the table, by name. And it offers a pattern for ordinary life. When someone says a thing you'd say differently, there are two easy roads: pretend they never said it, or shout it down. The Granth shows a third. Keep their words whole. Then answer, beside them, in your own voice.
screen: `THE BHAGATS, UNDER THEIR OWN NAMES.` · `A GURU'S VERSE BESIDE A BHAGAT'S.` · `NOT CUT OR SMOOTHED: BOTH VISIBLE.` · `A THIRD ROAD: KEEP IT WHOLE, THEN REPLY.` · then, large: `ANSWER, DON'T ERASE.`

segments.voice: The practice: reply kindly to someone. In the sit, think of a person who said something recently that you'd put differently. A message, a remark, an opinion. Let their words stand in your mind, whole, without trimming them to make them easier to dismiss. Then shape your reply. Not a correction shouted over them. A sentence beside theirs, in your own voice, that keeps the conversation going. Hold it until it's kind. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Nothing edited out. The Gurus kept the Bhagats' voices whole, and sometimes answered them in verses of their own, set beside them.
Your line: answer, don't erase. Today, when you disagree with someone, repeat back what they said fairly before you give your answer. Day seven hundred ninety-five.

796.title: Weaver, shoemaker, barber, king
796.hook: the Bhagats' trades read like a street; that's the point
796.howItsDone: Sikhs point to the Bhagats' different trades and castes as part of the Guru Granth Sahib's teaching that birth sets no limit on devotion, and the langar, where all sit together, puts the same teaching into practice.

segments.voice: Yesterday, nothing edited out: the Gurus kept the Bhagats' words whole and answered beside them. Your line was answer, don't erase. Did you repeat someone's words fairly before replying? Day seven hundred ninety-six.

A clatter from a loom in a doorway. Next door, someone bent over a shoe, stitching leather. Further on, a barber with a razor and a customer half-shaved. A farmer coming in from the fields with mud on his feet. And at the end of the road, a palace. Walk the names of the Bhagats in the Guru Granth Sahib and that's the street you're walking down: weaver, shoemaker, barber, king.
screen: `A LOOM IN A DOORWAY.` → `LEATHER, A RAZOR, A MUDDY FARMER.` → `A PALACE AT THE END OF THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: Some of these trades come from the Bhagats' own mouths. Kabir calls himself a weaver in his hymns, and works the loom into his songs. Namdev says he was born in the house of a calico printer. Ravidas says his family carried the dead cattle, work the caste order of his day looked down on. Others come from tradition: Sain the barber, Dhanna the farmer, Pipa the king who gave up his throne. Put them side by side and they don't read like a list of holy men from one class. They read like a street. That's the point. Ravidas's own hymns show a town that ranked people by birth, where a leather-worker's touch was counted as polluting. The Granth answers by putting the weaver's song, the leather worker's song and the king's song on the same pages, in the same raags, under the same honor. The barber's hymn is sung with the same reverence as the king's. Guru Nanak says it in his own words in Raag Asa, in paraphrase: recognize the light in everyone, and don't ask about caste; in the world beyond, there is no caste. So this isn't decoration. The mix of trades is the teaching, made visible. You can't hold the Guru Granth Sahib in your hands and keep the street out of it. And that runs both ways. The king isn't shut out either. Pipa's place there is as a devotee, beside the others, not above them.
screen: `IN THEIR OWN WORDS: LOOM, PRINT, CATTLE.` · `IN TRADITION: BARBER, FARMER, KING.` · `DON'T ASK ABOUT CASTE.` · `THE MIX IS THE TEACHING.` · then, large: `THE WHOLE STREET.`

segments.voice: For the practice, greet three different workers. In the sit, walk your own street the way we walked the Bhagats'. Whoever drives the bus, stacks the shelves, cuts hair, answers the phone, runs the office. Picture their faces as clearly as you can. Then choose three you'll actually see today, and decide to greet each one properly: eyes up, a real hello, a name if you can learn it. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Weaver. Kabir's own word for himself, at the head of a street of Bhagats: weaver, printer, leather worker, barber, farmer, king.
Your line: the whole street. Today, greet three people doing three different jobs, and look each of them in the eye. Day seven hundred ninety-six.

797.title: Bhagats in kirtan
797.hook: their hymns are sung like any other Gurbani
797.howItsDone: In gurdwaras, ragis sing the Bhagats' shabads in kirtan alongside the Gurus' hymns, in the raag the Granth assigns them, and the congregation listens and bows in the same way.

segments.voice: Yesterday, weaver, shoemaker, barber, king: the Bhagats' trades read like a street. Your line was the whole street. Did you greet someone whose work you usually walk past? Day seven hundred ninety-seven.

The harmonium is already breathing when the door opens. Three ragis sit on the low platform, one at the tabla, and the room is half full: a grandmother with a plastic bag of fruit, two teenagers near the back, a man who came straight from a night shift. The shabad on the screen ends, the tabla settles, and a new one begins. Same raag, same melody family, same people bowing their heads. Nobody in the room stops to ask who wrote it. If you glance at the heading, though, the name isn't a Guru's. It's Kabir's. Today: the Bhagats in kirtan.
screen: `THE HARMONIUM IS ALREADY PLAYING.` → `A NEW SHABAD BEGINS.` → `THE HEADING SAYS KABIR.`

segments.voice: Start with how the Granth is built. The hymns are arranged by raag, the musical mode they're meant to be sung in. Asa, Gauri, Sorath, Dhanasri. When the Gurus' hymns in a raag are done, the Bhagats' hymns follow in that same raag. Kabir in Gauri. Ravidas in Gauri too. Farid in Asa, as we saw a few weeks back. They aren't kept in an appendix at the back. They live in the same rooms as the Gurus' words, set to the same music. Then look at the heading. Each Bhagat hymn is marked with its raag and the Bhagat's name, often with ji added, a word of respect. That small mark tells the singer what to sing and the listener whose voice is speaking. It doesn't tell anyone to sing it differently. So in kirtan, a ragi can move from a hymn of Guru Arjan straight into one of Namdev, and the tabla doesn't change its manners. The Rahao line, the pause line that holds the hymn's center, gets sung as the refrain, the same way. When the shabad ends, people bow the same way. This is the heart of today. Sikhs call the hymns of the Granth bani, or gurbani, the Guru's word. The Bhagats' hymns are also called bhagat bani, which names whose voice it is, but they are read and sung as part of the Guru, not as quotations borrowed from outside. A Sikh singing Kabir isn't stepping out of the Guru's house for a minute. The whole book is the house. That's why the Bhagats are hard to spot in a gurdwara unless you read the heading. Their place isn't marked by a separate stage, only by a name.
screen: `THE GRANTH IS ARRANGED BY RAAG.` · `BHAGAT HYMNS SIT IN THE SAME RAAGS.` · `THE HEADING NAMES THE VOICE.` · `SUNG AND BOWED TO THE SAME WAY.` · then, large: `ALL GURBANI.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen to a Bhagat's shabad. For the sit, carry one Bhagat line from these weeks, in your own words: Parmanand's question, what did all that hearing change, or Surdas's single line about the company you keep. Let it ride the breath, in and out, the way a refrain comes back in kirtan. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out instead. Later today, find a recording of a Bhagat's shabad and listen once, all the way through, before checking whose it is. The bell holds the time.
Bhagats in kirtan. The Bhagats' hymns sit in the same raags as the Gurus' hymns, and they're sung, heard and bowed to the same way.
Your line: all gurbani. Today, when you hear or read any hymn from the Granth, look for the name in the heading, and then notice that the singing doesn't change. Day seven hundred ninety-seven.

798.title: One Bhagat a day
798.hook: a week of reading a different Bhagat each morning
798.howItsDone: Some Sikhs read from the Granth each day, and some keep a sehaj path, a slow reading of the whole Granth over time; a reader may also return to favorite shabads by their ang number.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Bhagats in kirtan: same raag, same refrain, same bow. Your line was all gurbani. Did you catch a name in a heading? Day seven hundred ninety-eight.

Seven sticky notes on the bathroom mirror. Each one has a name and a page number in marker: Ramanand. Bhikhan. Jaidev. Farid. A week of mornings, one voice per morning, before the phone gets a turn. It's the end of a week here too, so today does two jobs. It looks back at the voices of these seven days. And it hands over a small plan for the next seven: one Bhagat a day.
screen: `SEVEN NOTES ON A MIRROR.` → `ONE NAME EACH MORNING.` → `A WEEK BACK, A WEEK AHEAD.`

segments.voice: First, the week behind us. Satta and Balvand, the minstrels whose Var, tradition says, was sung after a quarrel was forgiven. The saloks headed with Mardana's name, words to a friend. Sundar's Sadd, Guru Amar Das asking for singing, not weeping. The Gurus answering voices they would put differently, rather than erasing them. The trades of the Bhagats, reading like a whole street. And yesterday, all of it sung as gurbani. Now the week ahead. The Granth is long, and a reader can stand at the front of it and not know where to begin. So here's a doorway the size of a morning. The ang, the page number, is the address. Day one, Ramanand in Raag Basant, Ang 1195: a home colored with love. Day two, Bhikhan in Sorath, Ang 659: the Name as medicine. Day three, Jaidev in Gujri, Ang 526, the old poet. Day four, Farid in Asa, Ang 488: the heart and the lips. Day five, Parmanand and Surdas, side by side on Ang 1253. Day six, Ravidas in Gauri, Ang 345, the city without sorrow he calls Begampura. Day seven, a handful of Kabir's saloks, near the end of the book. Each reading is short. Some are a few lines. Read it slowly, once, in Gurmukhi if you can, in a translation if you can't. Then stop. The point isn't to cover ground. It's to sit with one voice long enough to hear how it speaks: Farid's longing, Kabir's sharp edge, Ravidas's dream of a city. Read one a day, and by the end of the week these names stop being a list and become people.
screen: `A WEEK OF VOICES, LOOKED BACK ON.` · `THE ANG IS THE ADDRESS.` · `SEVEN MORNINGS, SEVEN BHAGATS.` · `READ ONE SLOWLY, THEN STOP.` · then, large: `ONE A DAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read a Bhagat today. If you can, open to one of those angs now, read a few lines slowly, and close it before the sit. If you can't, let the sit hold Ramanand's line in your own words: why go out looking, when home is colored with love. Breathe with it. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. When a thought pulls you toward the day's to-do list, let the line call you back. The bell holds the time.
One Bhagat a day. A week of mornings, a different Bhagat each morning, read slowly, with the ang as the address.
Your line: one a day. Tonight, write tomorrow's Bhagat and ang on a note and leave it where your morning starts. Day seven hundred ninety-eight.

screen: `DAY 798 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: WHICH VOICE SPEAKS TO YOU.`

fork.setup: it's morning, the Granth is open to a Bhagat's hymn, and you have five minutes. what do you do?
options: read as many hymns as you can before time runs out.
read one hymn slowly, once, and stop.
save it for a free weekend.
fork.reveal: the plan is one voice a day, read slowly, so the names become people rather than a list.

original.note: Gurmukhi: ang, a page of the Guru Granth Sahib; also the word for a limb of the body.

trapdoor: what you thought: a reading plan.
what it means: one Bhagat each morning for a week, read slowly, so each voice becomes a person.
what a scholar hears: readers use the ang to find a hymn, the way an address finds a house, so a reading plan can be a list of names and angs.

sources.ref: Salok Kabir, near the end of the Granth
